The agreement will empower Alaska, a company based in Seattle, to extend its reach into high-yielding markets like San Francisco and Los Angeles. Both corporate boards unanimously endorsed the transaction, through which Alaska will procure Virgin America at a rate of $57 (£40) per share. Regrettably, Sir Richard Branson, the founder of Virgin, acknowledged his inability to thwart the deal. This marks the first consolidation in the US commercial airline sector since the merger of US Airways and American Airlines in 2013, forming the largest airline globally. Virgin America, representing approximately 1.5% of domestic flight capacity in the United States, was introduced on the US stock market in 2014 as a subsidiary of Virgin Group headquartered in London. In a blog post on the company's website, Sir Richard expressed his melancholy over the merger with another entity. Due to his non-American status, the US Department of Transportation required him to convert some of his Virgin America shares into non-voting shares, diminishing his ability to influence any acquisition attempts. Consequently, he found himself powerless to prevent the consolidation. Sir Richard highlighted that consolidation is an unstoppable trend, with the top four airlines now controlling over 80% of the US aviation market. Alaska and its regional partners, constituting around 5% of domestic flight capacity in the US, cater to over 100 destinations across the United States, Canada, Costa Rica, and Mexico. Pending approval from US governmental authorities and Virgin America shareholders, both companies anticipate finalizing the transaction by January 1st, 2017. Brad Tilden, who serves as the chairman and chief executive officer of Alaska Air Group, expressed optimism about providing customers with enhanced travel options through an expanded network and a substantial presence in California. The recent investment announcement will ensure the continuation of numerous job positions at the Sunderland factory, which is responsible for manufacturing the current Juke, Qashqai, Note, and electric Leaf models. Nissan stated that this financial commitment provides stability for our Sunderland plant beyond the year 2020. Chancellor George Osborne expressed his delight at this significant development, highlighting its importance as a demonstration of the UK's position as a leading global hub for car production. Last year, the Sunderland plant produced 500,000 cars, solidifying its status as the largest car manufacturing facility in the UK, according to Nissan. Prof David Bailey from Aston Business School noted that Nissan's Sunderland plant alone produces more vehicles than the entire Italian automotive industry. This new investment will safeguard 6,700 positions at the plant and over 27,000 jobs within its supply chain. Tony Burke, assistant general secretary of Unite union, welcomed Nissan's decision to produce the new Juke model in the UK instead of overseas plants. This move underscores the industry's confidence in the skilled and dedicated workforce present across the UK automotive sector. Paul Wilcox, chairman of Nissan Europe, described the Sunderland plant as potentially the most efficient in Europe and globally. Despite a slowdown in demand from Russia and China, Wilcox emphasized the strong performance of the car market in western Europe and particularly in the UK. While acknowledging global market volatility, he noted a slight increase in demand. Data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders revealed that UK car production reached a seven-year peak of 793,642 vehicles in the first half of this year – equivalent to three cars being produced every minute. A destructive cyclone named 03A has caused significant casualties and damage, resulting in the deaths of thousands of livestock and the destruction of hundreds of homes. While the cyclone has passed, officials warn that heavy rainfall is still expected.

Puntland, a semi-autonomous region within Somalia, is heavily dependent on livestock herding and fishing for its economy. The tropical cyclone swept through various districts along the east coast, including Eyl, Beyla, Dangorayo, Hafun, and Alula on the Horn of Africa. According to Puntland's Interior Minister Abdullahi Ahmed, the confirmed death toll stands at 140, but fears are that it may rise to 300 as many individuals are still missing.

Difficulties in delivering aid have been exacerbated by heavy flooding rendering many roads impassable. Entire villages, homes, buildings, and boats have been destroyed by the storm. Makeshift shelters have been constructed to accommodate displaced individuals. The government has requested assistance from international aid organizations for air-drops of essential supplies such as clean water, non-perishable food, tents, blankets, and medicines. Ten doctors and two ambulances are providing medical care to those in need.

In a show of solidarity, Somalia's government has pledged $1 million towards aiding communities impacted by the cyclone. Prime Minister Abdi Farah Shirdon expressed shared sorrow with affected communities.

The artist responsible for the installation in question has claimed to be the first individual to uncover Banksy's identity by capturing a photograph of him in 2004. Peter Dean Rickards acquired the wall adorned with the mural from a bar in Kingston, deliberately destroying it. This exhibit, hosted at the New Art Exchange, commemorates 50 years of Jamaican independence. Rachel Barrett, the curator of the showcase, remarked that the general population in Jamaica struggled to grasp the significance of the mural as a work of art. Through his artistry, Peter Dean Rickards challenges the superficial value attached to celebrities within society.

The mural in question depicted Banksy's Balloon Girl and was estimated to have been painted by Banksy himself in Kingston during 2004. Reportedly, Mr. Rickards managed to capture photographs of Banksy at work during his time in Kingston. In 2008, the Mail on Sunday published an article claiming to have identified Banksy as Robin Gunningham, a former public school student, based on one of Rickards' photos. Additionally, reports from 2008 alleged that Mr. Rickards allowed a dog to defecate on the artwork post his acquisition of the wall.

A video showcasing Mr. Rickards dismantling the mural plays repeatedly alongside the exhibit in Nottingham. The shattered wall is positioned in one corner of a space designed to resemble the garage where it was stored for numerous years following its removal. In the exhibition notes, Mr. Rickards is quoted expressing disdain towards Banksy's popularity among white individuals in the UK who are willing to pay exorbitant amounts for his works. The exhibition, entitled "I Is AnOther," will run until 8 December.

Commissioned as part of an Australian road safety campaign, the remarkably realistic sculpture known as Graham features a head resembling a boulder, feet resembling tangled tree roots, and a chest reminiscent of a wrinkled battering ram. Renowned artist Patricia Piccinini collaborated with a leading trauma surgeon and a road crash investigation expert to create this artwork. The Transport Accident Commission (TAC) stated that Graham was specifically designed to emphasize human vulnerability on the road. Graham possesses a robust skull, a neck seamlessly blending into his torso, and an inflatable chest mimicking airbags. Constructed from silicone, glass fibre, resin, and human hair, Graham embodies a fusion of art and science in Piccinini's words.

The eyes serve as the focal point of Graham's composition, allowing viewers to establish an emotional connection with him. Joe Calafiore, CEO of TAC, highlighted the stark contrast between surviving collisions with inanimate objects versus vehicles due to the higher speeds and forces involved in the latter scenario. With cars advancing more rapidly than humans, Graham serves as a symbol illustrating the imperative need for enhancing all facets of our road infrastructure to mitigate human errors.

Graham's name originated as a working title that resonated with TAC due to his portrayal as an ordinary Australian man. He can be visited at the State Library of Victoria or observed online for those interested in exploring this thought-provoking sculpture further.

The Tri Ceffyl Bach Nursery in Amlwch was closed as a precaution last Thursday due to the detection of three cases of E. coli O157 in children. Testing has been offered to both children and adults, with public health officers and environmental health teams from Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board and Anglesey Council currently conducting investigations into the outbreak.

Dr. Chris Whiteside, a consultant in communicable disease control for Public Health Wales, emphasized the need for caution given the highly contagious nature of the infection, particularly among young children. Nursery staff, as well as individuals in close contact with those who are unwell or at higher risk, are undergoing testing as a preventive measure.

Identifying the definitive source of the outbreak can be challenging, as E. coli O157 spreads easily through contaminated food, infected individuals, farm animals, or water sources. Therefore, strict adherence to personal hygiene practices is crucial to prevent further transmission of the infection.

Symptoms of E. coli O157 can range from mild diarrhea and stomach cramps to severe bloody diarrhea and fever. The incubation period typically lasts between one to 14 days, with most cases becoming symptomatic within three to four days. Individuals infected with E. coli O157 may experience illness for up to two weeks.

As part of containment measures, individuals must receive two consecutive negative tests for E. coli O157 taken at least 48 hours apart before being permitted to return to the nursery. The ongoing investigation aims to uncover the source of the outbreak and implement appropriate control measures to protect the health and safety of all individuals involved.

The animals employ echolocation to hunt their prey, emitting clicks and buzzes to detect the echoes bouncing off potential targets. A team of researchers from Aarhus University in Denmark have observed a fascinating phenomenon - these animals have the ability to adjust the width of their sound beam, akin to changing the focus of a flashlight, as they close in on their prey. This shift in sound beam width could potentially prevent porpoises, whales, and dolphins from evading capture during hunting.

Lead researcher Danuta Wisniewska and her team conducted experiments with harbour porpoises in a semi-natural enclosure along the Danish coast. By equipping the porpoises with sound-detecting tags and strategically placing microphones around their habitat, the researchers were able to study how these animals direct their sound energy. The porpoises were enticed to hunt by dropping fish into the water, allowing the researchers to observe their hunting techniques.

The study revealed that porpoises can expand their sound beam by up to 50% during the final phase of attack, demonstrating a remarkable ability to switch between narrow and wide sound beams. This flexibility is controlled by a fatty structure in their forehead known as the melon, which acts as a type of sound lens. The harbour porpoises involved in this study had previously been rescued from fishing nets, inspiring the researchers to explore new methods of using sound to prevent these animals from inadvertently becoming entangled in fishing gear.

In the bustling Shia district of Karrada in Baghdad, two explosions occurred within minutes of each other during the peak afternoon rush hour. The first detonation targeted a restaurant and a bakery at al-Andalus Square, while the second blast occurred outside a court near a prominent police headquarters. This wave of violence adds to the more than 240 casualties from recent militant attacks in Iraq, as reported by Rami Ruhayem for BBC News.

The aftermath of the explosions was devastating, with many vehicles left charred and destroyed. Among the wreckage was a small Iranian-made yellow taxi that had been completely incinerated, leaving only a skeletal metal frame where the interior once stood. Littered across the debris was a teddy bear covered in dust, likely from the nearby building that bore the brunt of the blast. The structural integrity of the building seemed compromised, with shattered glass, severe damage to the ground floor restaurant and bakery, and residents on upper floors gazing down in a state of detached resignation.

The recent surge in violence in Baghdad and surrounding areas has been attributed to Sunni insurgents affiliated with al-Qaeda. On 23 July alone, a series of bombings and shootings resulted in over 100 fatalities. The attacks on al-Andalus Square further intensified the chaos, causing more than 50 injuries in addition to numerous fatalities.

Eyewitness accounts painted a harrowing picture of the scene, with one police officer describing a minibus containing six lifeless passengers. Tragically, several law enforcement officials were also among the casualties. While initial reports suggested that one of the bombings was carried out by a suicide bomber, local media outlets indicated that both attacks were likely orchestrated by individuals intent on causing harm and destruction.

Subsequently, authorities have commenced a search of the premises located at Icknield Way, Luton. Two individuals, aged 66 and 39, from Luton have been apprehended on suspicion of murder and are presently in police custody. Updates on this case and others from Bedfordshire Police are forthcoming.

Preliminary assessments indicate that the discovered remains likely belong to a female, although formal identification is pending. The elder suspect had previously been detained on charges related to aiding an offender and obstructing a lawful burial. Additionally, a 71-year-old individual from Port Glasgow, Scotland is currently on bail for suspected involvement in the same crimes.

Detective Inspector Jerry Waite of the Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire major crime unit disclosed that recent investigations led them to the garden where excavation activities began last Monday. Skeletal remains were uncovered during this process. While formal identification is pending, the family of Natalia Doherty has been notified as authorities strongly believe that the remains may belong to her.

According to detectives, prior to her demise, Ms. Doherty had traveled to Luton to visit her deceased ex-husband, Gerald, at the Regents Arms on Hastings Street. DI Waite urged anyone acquainted with the pair around Ms. Doherty's last confirmed sighting on April 15, 2003 to come forward and provide any relevant information. Specifically, individuals who had interactions with them in Luton between February and April 2003 are urged to share their knowledge with authorities.

Recognizing this reality is crucial in addressing the issue effectively and promoting rehabilitation among inmates.

The judiciary declined to provide an active sheriff for an interview on the matter, but former sheriff Peter Gillam offered insights from his time on the bench. Serving as a sheriff from 1991 until 2013, Gillam emphasized that the discrepancies in sentencing practices underscored the judiciary's autonomy. He acknowledged the existence of a board tasked with advising judges on sentencing matters but stressed that each judge operates independently and applies their own unique approach based on personal beliefs and professional judgment. While a certain level of consistency is maintained through the oversight of an Appeal Court, Gillam argued that diversity among judges is essential and should be respected. He highlighted the significance of local knowledge, individual discretion, and trust in judges' ability to make informed decisions tailored to specific cases.

United Airlines experienced a network connectivity problem which resulted in flight disruptions on June 2nd. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed that the airline successfully resolved the issue by 10:00 ET (14:00 GMT). This incident adds to a series of technical difficulties faced by the company, such as the accidental sale of first-class seats for $100 (Â£65) in February. In response to the recent connectivity problem, United Airlines issued an apology to customers and assured that efforts were being made to rectify the situation.

The network issue affected approximately 3,500 flights, leading to complaints from passengers regarding delays and lack of information on social media platforms. The frustration felt by customers was evident in tweets like the one from Jeralyn Novak, who declared they would never fly with United Airlines again. Journalist Betsy Fischer Martin also shared her disappointment with the situation, describing the outage as akin to having the plug pulled on their computers.

Following the lifting of the FAA order, United Airlines began the process of recovering and restoring flight operations. However, reports surfaced of long queues at airports nationwide. This recent incident is part of a pattern of technical problems encountered by the airline in recent months, including an instance where transatlantic flights were sold at significantly reduced prices due to a computer glitch. Despite facing criticism for not honoring these fares, United Airlines attributed the error to a third-party software provider.

While United Airlines is not alone in facing technical challenges, with American Airlines also experiencing disruptions due to software issues, the incident underscores the importance of robust IT systems within the aviation industry.

The office of Secretary Perry confirmed that he was engaged in conversation with two Russian pranksters. These individuals, identified as Vladimir Kuznetsov and Alexei Stolyaro, are known for targeting prominent politicians and celebrities. Previous victims of their pranks include Arizona Senator John McCain and singer Elton John. In this instance, the pranksters posed as Ukrainian Prime Minister Volodymyr Groysman.

Energy Department spokeswoman Shaylyn Hynes noted that Secretary Perry is the most recent target of these Russian pranksters. She highlighted their tendency to prank high-ranking officials and celebrities who support agendas that diverge from their respective governments. In this case, the discussion centered around the energy security of Ukraine, according to Ms. Hynes.

The prank call took place on a date subsequent to Secretary Perry hosting the Ukrainian president and his delegation in Washington. The call was arranged following a request received by Mr. Perry's office on 12 July, with the actual conversation occurring one week later. The topics covered during the call included US coal exports to Ukraine, Russian hackers, a proposed energy pipeline in the Baltic Sea, and a potentially fictitious fuel source generated from animal manure and homemade alcohol. The pranksters claimed that this biological fuel had been developed by Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko.

During the conversation, Secretary Perry expressed concern about the impact of US withdrawal from the Paris climate accord on relations with Ukraine. This accord, from which President Trump announced US withdrawal, was mentioned in the context of maintaining positive relations with Ukraine.

It is noteworthy that Mr. Perry, a former Texas governor who withdrew from the 2012 presidential race after struggling to recall names of departments he sought to eliminate during a debate, found himself inadvertently engaging in a conversation with these Russian pranksters.

The arrest of Zdravko Mamic, the chairman of Dinamo Zagreb, and his brother Zoran, the club's coach, upon their return from the team's summer camp has raised allegations of fraud amounting to 118 million kunas ($17.3 million, £11.1 million) since 2008. The brothers have vehemently asserted their innocence and are determined to defend themselves against the charges.

The anti-corruption investigators have implicated a senior official from the Croatian Football Federation, a tax inspector, and the Mamic brothers in bribery, tax evasion, and other criminal activities. Reports from Croatian and German media suggest that they are accused of receiving illicit payments from player transfers at Dinamo Zagreb, resulting in losses of 12 million kunas ($1.8 million, £1.1 million) to the state.

Following police raids at the club's premises, the football federation offices, and the homes of the Mamic brothers, as well as the detention of two other individuals, efforts are being made to keep the suspects in custody pending a court decision in Zagreb.

Zdravko Mamic, a prominent figure in Croatian football, has refuted the allegations against him as baseless and politically motivated. Despite the ongoing investigation, Dinamo Zagreb has expressed its unwavering support for the brothers, with a statement on the club's website affirming their belief in their innocence.

The timing of these events coincided with Dinamo Zagreb's preparations for the upcoming season in Slovenia. As the most successful club in Croatian football history with 17 titles and 10 consecutive championships, this scandal has cast a shadow over their legacy.

In November 2013, Essex Police received information from the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre (CEOP) regarding an individual named Martin Goldberg. However, it was not until September of the following year that authorities realized Goldberg's occupation as a teacher. The delay in this discovery was attributed by Essex's police commissioner to an unclear phrase, the specifics of which were not disclosed. It is believed that a misinterpretation of this ambiguous phrase by CEOP contributed to the confusion in passing on the information, as noted by Nick Alston. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) is currently examining this particular aspect as part of their investigation.

Martin Goldberg, who served as deputy head of Thorpe Hall School in Southend, tragically passed away the day after being interviewed by the police. Prior to his death, his name had appeared on a list of 35 intelligence packages shared with Essex Police by CEOP ten months earlier. This information had originated from Canadian authorities in 2012 following an investigation into a company distributing inappropriate content involving children. Despite this, Goldberg was not flagged as a high-risk individual to Essex Police initially.

Upon realizing Goldberg's profession, law enforcement sought a search warrant - which was ultimately denied - and visited his residence. Nick Alston acknowledged that Essex Police has since revised its protocols in response to this case. Going forward, immediate occupational checks will be conducted when receiving intelligence to determine any potential risks associated with individuals working with children.

In light of ongoing inquiries by the IPCC, a spokesperson for CEOP declined to provide further insights on the matter.

The company reported that criminals have been utilizing the infamous Angler Exploit malware tool to target thousands of users on a daily basis. The specific focus of these attacks has been on customers of hosting provider Limestone Networks. Cisco has taken action by issuing a patch and providing guidance on how users can protect themselves; however, analysts are skeptical that this will completely eradicate Angler attacks. Security expert Graham Cluley cautioned against expecting Cisco's actions to deliver a fatal blow to the Angler Exploit Kit, but acknowledged that it has certainly caused some disruption to the criminals' activities.

Cisco's security team uncovered this fraudulent activity as part of a comprehensive investigation into Angler, which is considered one of the most sophisticated and alarming hacking tools currently in circulation. This malware exploits vulnerabilities in Flash, Java, and other browser plug-ins to infiltrate systems. Once inside, it can hold computers hostage, demanding a ransom in exchange for restoring access to the device. Approximately half of the Angler attacks analyzed by Cisco were found to target servers connected to the US-based hosting provider, affecting an estimated 90,000 individuals daily and generating over $30 million in illicit profits annually.

Security expert Ken Munro praised Cisco's efforts as an effective means of combating malware by disrupting critical communication channels that the exploit relies on. However, he warned that malware authors are likely to adapt their tools in response to such countermeasures, leading to an ongoing battle in a slightly altered form. Cisco's estimation puts the global revenue generated by Angler attacks at potentially over $60 million each year.

In 1988, the Primary Five class of Primate Dixon Primary School in Coalisland completed reading Roald Dahl's book "Danny, the Champion of the World" and decided to reach out to the renowned author. Shortly thereafter, they received a response from Dahl himself, known for creating iconic characters such as Willy Wonka, Miss Trunchbull, and the Twits. The Irish News reported that Dahl's letter, addressed to teacher James Maye and his class, praised their teacher's compassionate approach in contrast to his own experiences. The letter included a poem that humorously highlighted the differences in teaching methods, with lines such as "There's no whacks on the bum, When you can't do a sum, Instead you get strawberries and cream."

Despite the significance of this correspondence, the letter and poem were stored away in a drawer for nearly three decades, collecting dust until 2012 when Vice Principal Siobhan Murphy discovered them while cleaning out an old desk. The school's principal, Sean Dillon, shared that upon realizing the literary treasure they had in their possession, they immediately recognized its value. Further investigation revealed that the unpublished poem had later been included in the 'Roald Dahl Treasury,' a 1997 collection of Dahl's unreleased works.

To commemorate the centenary of Roald Dahl's birth, the letter and poem were put on display at Primate Dixon Primary School. Sean Dillon expressed great pride in the school's connection to the beloved author, whose books have left an indelible mark on countless childhoods worldwide. With over 200 million copies sold in 59 languages, Dahl's work continues to be a cornerstone of children's literature.

The Lost Songs of St Kilda quickly sold out upon its release, making it the fastest-selling posthumous artist debut in history. Recorded in an Edinburgh care home by pensioner Trevor Morrison using a modest £3 microphone, the album features tracks that have been reworked by esteemed composers such as Sir James Macmillan, Craig Armstrong, Christopher Duncan, Rebecca Dale, and Francis Macdonald of Teenage Fanclub. To mark the album's release, Sir James embarked on an eight-hour boat journey to perform a special piano concert on the islands, marking the first time music had been heard on St Kilda since its evacuation in 1930. This event also marked the first occasion a piano had been brought to the island, requiring disassembly and reassembly for transport.

Sir James expressed his delight in being part of the project, praising Trevor Morrison's rendition of the old St Kilda songs for their poignant and haunting qualities. Morrison's playing showcased a sensitivity and artistry that effectively communicated the beauty and simplicity of the lost music. The collaboration with various Scottish musicians and composers from diverse genres provided unique perspectives on the original tunes.

As a 10-year-old during World War Two on the west coast island of Bute, Trevor Morrison learned to play the piano from a former St Kilda resident. Despite facing health challenges while residing in a care home, Morrison managed to recall the melodies his teacher had shared with him. Stuart McKenzie, a volunteer at the care home, offered to record these songs. Before his passing in 2012, Morrison expressed his gratitude towards those involved in preserving these tunes that had haunted him throughout his life. His wish was for these few melodies from the forgotten isles to be safeguarded and given a future. The last inhabitants left St Kilda on 29 August 1930 due to the extreme hardships of life on the remote archipelago.

The variance in shape of the vertebrae is attributed to the development of a lesion within the intervertebral disc, which occurs in the transition from quadrupedal to bipedal locomotion during human evolution. This discovery has significant implications for identifying individuals at risk of developing spinal issues, as suggested by researchers. The collaborative study, published in BMC Evolutionary Biology, engaged scientists from Scotland, Canada, and Iceland in the examination of chimpanzee, orangutan, and ancient human skeletal remains to explore the correlation between vertebral morphology, upright movement, and spinal health. Professor Mark Collard, affiliated with the University of Aberdeen and Simon Fraser University in Canada, asserted that the investigation provided valuable insights into the health and lifestyles of our ancestors. By analyzing the skeletons, researchers gained insight into how humans adapted to bipedalism over time. Notably, individuals with spinal disc abnormalities exhibited vertebrae more akin to those of chimpanzees than humans without such issues. It was observed that these individuals presented with Schmorl's nodes - small hernias that can manifest within the intervertebral disc due to lower back stress. The imperfections in evolution have resulted in variations among humans over millennia. Professor Collard explained that certain individuals may possess vertebrae less suited for bipedalism due to pathological conditions. The researchers posit that their findings could inform modern healthcare practices and serve as a predictive tool for identifying potential health risks.

A spokesperson for Guernsey's Policy Council expressed interest in monitoring developments in Jersey, while the Guernsey States Assembly and Constitution Committee announced plans to discuss the report in an upcoming meeting.

The decision to divide the role of seneschal in Sark, where one individual held both positions as chief judge and president of Chief Pleas, serves as a recent example prompting scrutiny of dual roles within legal and political systems.

Sergeant Robert Bye was posthumously awarded the Victoria Cross for his exemplary conduct during the initial day of the 3rd Battle of Ypres on July 31, 1917. A commemorative paving stone inscribed with his name will be ceremoniously placed at Ynysangharad War Memorial Park in Pontypridd. Despite receiving a hero's welcome upon his return, Sgt. Bye pursued a career as a miner until his passing in 1962.

The citation accompanying his WWI Victoria Cross details how his courageous actions led to the capture or elimination of 70 German soldiers. The 3rd Battle of Ypres, also known as The Battle of Passchendaele, resulted in over 300,000 allied casualties, equating to approximately 35 casualties per meter gained.

During the battle's inception, Sgt. Bye's company successfully breached the lightly defended German front line but encountered significant challenges when met with machine gun fire from a heavily fortified blockhouse system along the support line. Despite facing adversity, Sgt. Bye single-handedly navigated to the rear of the nearest blockhouse and neutralized the threat by throwing a hand grenade. Dodging enemy fire from a neighboring blockhouse, he managed to silence that post as well, enabling the Welsh Guards to secure their predetermined objectives.

King George V presented Sgt. Bye with his Victoria Cross on September 5, 1917, at Buckingham Palace. Following his return home to Penrhiwceiber, celebrations adorned the streets with bunting and schools closed in commemoration of his courageous actions.

Representatives from the Welsh Guards will attend the upcoming ceremony to honor Sgt. Robert Bye VC. Major Karl Dawson praised Sgt. Bye's bravery and dedication as emblematic of the qualities exhibited by Guardsmen in present-day operations, emphasizing the importance of learning from such experiences and upholding the tradition of honoring brave individuals within the Welsh family heritage.

They described her as "our princess, our general, and more importantly, our friend" and expressed their ongoing grief over her passing. The legacy she left behind as Princess Leia will always be honored and cherished by the Star Wars community. Over her illustrious career in the Star Wars franchise, Fisher appeared in four films beginning with Episode IV in 1977 and concluding with Star Wars: The Force Awakens in 2015. According to data released by Destatis, seasonally adjusted exports in Germany experienced a significant decline of 2.6% compared to the previous month, marking the largest monthly drop since August 2015. This comes amidst a series of concerning economic indicators for German manufacturing, with industrial orders showing minimal growth in July and output experiencing the most significant decrease in nearly two years. Germany's economic strength has long been driven by robust trade relationships with other nations. Despite the recent slowdown, the country still maintained a trade surplus of €19.4 billion in July. However, demand for German goods saw a notable decrease from countries outside of the European Union. Exports to third countries, including China, Russia, Japan, and the US, fell by 13.8% compared to July 2015, while exports to EU countries outside of the eurozone, such as Britain, dropped by 8.8%. Economists such as Carsten Brzeski from ING and Ralph Solveen from Commerzbank expressed concerns about the impact of these weak trade figures on overall economic growth in Germany. Brzeski noted that the disappointing performance in July may lead to discussions about potential fiscal stimulus in the future, while Solveen pointed out that exports are unlikely to be a key driver of the German economy in the upcoming months due to factors such as a sluggish global economy and diminishing effects from the weaker euro. Northumbria Police has announced changes to the operating hours of all front desks, with the exception of the Sunderland location, which will now only be open during daytime hours starting on Monday. This decision comes as a response to the increasing trend of people reporting crimes online or over the phone rather than in person at a police station. The force believes that this move will result in cost savings.

However, the union Unison has expressed concerns about the tight timescale for implementing these changes and has called for a consultation process. Unison's regional organiser, Peter Chapman, has warned that these plans could lead to job redundancies. While Unison acknowledges the need to reconsider how police stations provide services in the future, they argue that the current proposals are too radical and the timeline is too restrictive.

Unison is urging Northumbria Police to halt the current proposals and engage in a more thorough and inclusive consultation with all stakeholders. Despite these concerns, Northumbria Police has assured that the changes will not impact officer availability and that the savings generated will be reinvested into operational policing and enhancing accessibility, including additional funding for 101 contact centres.

Chief Constable Steve Ashman emphasized that these changes are being made in response to ongoing austerity measures and budget cuts, which have necessitated difficult decisions. He highlighted the importance of delivering high-quality services to communities while adapting to public preferences for reporting incidents conveniently from their homes. The force aims to maintain a visible police presence on the streets while modernizing its approach to meet evolving needs.

If left unaddressed, bracken would spread extensively throughout the dune system at Murlough on the County Down coast, threatening the delicate balance of the dune heath habitat. This habitat, encompassing 16% of the total in the UK, is situated within the 700-acre site located between Dundrum and Newcastle. It serves as a crucial ecosystem supporting a diverse array of plant and animal species, as well as a rich population of moths and butterflies. Murlough is home to 700 moth species and 23 butterfly species. The removal of bracken is undertaken with the dual purpose of aiding these species and managing the habitat. According to Patrick Lynch, a conservation ranger at the site, bracken has the potential to become invasive, forming dense thickets that inhibit growth underneath. To address this issue, almost 30 acres of bracken are cleared annually by the National Trust, which oversees Murlough. This removal process involves a combination of rolling and spraying techniques. In addition to manual removal methods, the site is managed using livestock. Cattle and 10 Exmoor ponies are allowed to graze in the area to help control the growth of bracken and promote the flourishing of other plant species. According to the report titled "Caught Short," India has an alarming number of 48 million stunted children under the age of five, ranking the highest globally. Following India, Nigeria and Pakistan rank second and third with 10.3 and 9.8 million stunted children, respectively. Stunting, a result of malnutrition during the critical first two years of a child's life, has profound and often irreversible consequences on both physical and cognitive development. In addition to food scarcity, factors such as inadequate sanitation and contaminated drinking water contribute significantly to malnutrition, ultimately leading to stunted growth in children. Poor access to toilets, clean water, and proper hygiene practices play a pivotal role in this crisis. Chronic diarrhoea, frequently caused by unclean water and unsanitary conditions, is directly linked to malnutrition, accounting for a significant portion of stunting cases in early childhood. The report highlights that approximately 76 million individuals lack access to safe drinking water in India, while a staggering 774 million people do not have sufficient sanitation facilities. Tragically, around 140,000 children succumb to diarrhoea annually in India. Open defecation remains a prevalent health concern in the country, with more than half a billion people engaging in this practice. Such unsanitary conditions not only facilitate the spread of deadly diseases but also increase children's vulnerability to infections like diarrhoea. Despite these challenges, there have been some improvements in reducing the prevalence of stunted children in India. The charity notes that while 48% of children were stunted in 2006, this figure decreased to 39% by 2014. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has prioritized efforts to ensure access to clean drinking water and adequate sanitation for all citizens as part of his government's agenda.
